description: Portable processor scenarios for the OpenAPI 3.0 binding-specification sibling. Configuration is named semantically; adapters normalize HTTP observations.

scenarios.description: A scalar query parameter uses the OpenAPI-declared query location and serialization rather than becoming a body field. [CO30-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
The first patch-looking edition beyond the accepted OpenAPI 3.0 set is refused rather than inferred compatible.

An OAS 3.0 binary schema carries exact raw bytes for a concrete image media type; the lane is schema-driven rather than restricted to application/octet-stream. [CO30-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
A non-canonical Base64 boundary value for an OAS 3.0 raw body refuses before dispatch. [CO30-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
Raw-body bytes are declaration-selected and never sniffed as JSON merely because their decoded spelling is JSON text. [CO30-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
A required raw body with no caller input refuses before dispatch like every other required request body.
An OAS 3.0 binary success response crosses the protocol-independent output boundary as canonical Base64 of its exact octets.

A dynamic form object is the envelope's one body value, independently of a same-named query parameter; no declaration trigger changes caller correspondence. [CO30-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
An exact schema-omitted OAS 3.0 non-JSON declaration carries request and response octets through the canonical Base64 application boundary. [CO30-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

OAS 3.0.4 is the edition where the 3.0 line first states the content interpretation ("The absence of all three of those fields is the equivalent of using content") and where Appendix E first appears. An urlencoded property with no Encoding Object therefore takes the content path there, which the OAS pairs with RFC 1866 Section 8.2.1, whose first escaping step replaces a space with +. OAS 3.0.0-3.0.3 state neither sentence and this specification states no path-selection rule for that line, so no scenario pins it. [CO30-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

expected.description: The 3.0 line reaches the content path from 3.0.4 onward. One permitted observation, not a set.

scenarios.description: No accepted 3.0 edition states a default contentType row for a part declaring no `type`, and this binding authors none. The missing fact is one concrete media type, so a required body carrying that part is context-required on the `propertyMedia` configuration point for `profile` before input consumption and dispatches nothing.

The whole OAS 3.0 line emits ONE body for a control-free urlencoded property, and this scenario is edition 3.0.0 of the five that state it. The Encoding Object writes contentType and no style, explode or allowReserved, so the content path governs: the object's JSON image rides as one field under the property's own name; the containing form layer percent-encodes whichever permitted JSON spelling is produced. Edition 3.0.0 states no lane-selection rule of its own; it reaches this behaviour through its own Section 4.1 patch-uniformity instruction together with 3.0.4, a 3.0.* version, whose Section 4.7.15.1.2 states that with all three fields absent "Encoding is to be based on contentType alone". A processor that keys any part of this on the PATCH component of the openapi field emits address's members as top-level fields (street=main%20st), discards the artifact's explicit contentType, and loses the field name the operation is built around; each of 3.0.0 through 3.0.3 forbids that distinction in its OWN Section 4.1, in the words "The patch version SHOULD NOT be considered by tooling, making no distinction between 3.0.0 and 3.0.1 for example" — 3.0.4 and the 3.1 editions carry the same sentence naming 3.1.0 and 3.1.1 instead, so the instruction governing an artifact that declares a 3.0-line patch is the one in that artifact's own edition. One fixed property mapping, with only §12.4's JSON-byte latitude. [CO30-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

scenarios.description: On the 3.0 line patternProperties is outside the Schema Object dialect and decides as if absent, while CO30-03 independently makes the envelope body the complete caller value without any dialect-keyed correspondence trigger. [CO30-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

On the 3.0 line if, dependentSchemas, and unevaluatedProperties are outside the Schema Object dialect and decide as if absent, while CO30-03 independently makes the envelope body the complete caller value without making correspondence dialect-dependent. [CO30-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

On the 3.0 line a `type: string` with `format: byte` is ALREADY the encoded characters — every accepted 3.0 edition's own Data Types format registry defines `byte` as "base64 encoded characters", 3.0.4's row citing [RFC 4648] Section 4 — so an exact non-JSON, non-form selection governed by that declaration carries the caller's string as artifact-encoded Base64 text, sent AS-IS. The OpenBindings raw-byte boundary decode does not run: artifact encoding and the OpenBindings boundary encoding are distinct, exactly as they are for the 3.1 `contentEncoding` lane this rule parallels. The lane is not gated on character-data media — application/pdf is outside that test — because here the ARTIFACT, not the media-type registration, is what declares the value to be characters. The wire body is therefore the string itself and not the three octets it encodes. [CO30-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

The form-part half of the same 3.0 cell, and its part default. 3.0.4's Encoding Object default-`contentType` table gives `string` with `format` "`binary` or `byte`" the default application/octet-stream, while 3.0.0 through 3.0.3's prose names only `binary` before "other primitive types"; under the editions' own Section 4.1 patch-uniformity instruction the line answers uniformly and 3.0.4 read under its own text fixes what the uniform answer is, so a `byte` part defaults to application/octet-stream on every 3.0 edition rather than to the primitive text/plain row. Its value is the caller's artifact-encoded Base64 text sent as-is — the contrast with the `binary` sibling, which takes the SAME default Content-Type while its value is the OpenBindings canonical Base64 boundary and emits the decoded octets, is carried by the shared format-byte-carriage case table rather than here, because one multipart body containing both parts cannot assert which part a Content-Type belongs to through a substring. 3.0.4 additionally equates a `byte` part with an Encoding Object whose `headers` field carries a Content-Transfer-Encoding schema requiring base64; this specification reads that equivalence as declaration semantics, so no such header is emitted for an artifact that does not declare one. [CO30-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
An unknown caller-envelope top-level key refuses before dispatch; only parameters and body are admitted.
A present non-object parameters member refuses before dispatch.
An unknown key inside the parameters member refuses before dispatch.
A cross-location name collision activates qualified mode for every parameter, so the bare name refuses before dispatch.
A well-formed caller envelope supplies colliding path and query parameters through their qualified keys and dispatches successfully.
A deepObject member value containing its structural ampersand delimiter refuses instead of percent-encoding the ambiguity.
The unified resolved-declaration proof follows $ref and allOf and excludes a form-style object member that declares only an object compound shape.
A schema-form Header Parameter value containing CR/LF refuses before an HTTP field is constructed.

A caller-supplied request Content-Encoding is admitted by the effective Header Parameter, but runtime encoder capability does not support its token. The condition is never skipped or sniffed: a request-side condition refuses before dispatch.

Content-coding implementations are runtime capabilities, not binding configuration points. The actual Content-Encoding field fixes the coding stack even when the governing Response Object declares no Header Object for it. An absent declaration therefore imposes no content-coding constraint and does not declare identity; the runtime decoder removes the coding before the selected media lane.
A governing non-Content-Type response Header Object declaring required true makes the actual header mandatory; absence is a loud response protocol error even for an empty body.
A non-empty response without Content-Type assumes application/octet-stream before ordinary declaration matching and crosses the raw boundary as canonical Base64.
A non-empty actual response with no governing Response Object is a loud protocol error; another status declaration cannot govern it.
A text/event-stream response remains unary under this binding: one HTTP body produces one application string rather than a predecessor streaming sequence.
The actual request and response Content-Encoding fields name identity, which needs no runtime codec: both stacks preserve the representation bytes unchanged.

Two concrete request-media entries preserve both declared alternatives, but the sole-concrete rule requires configuration.requestMedia before a required body can consume input; examples and supplied value shape select neither.
readOnly and writeOnly are application annotations: the binding preserves both supplied JSON members on the request wire instead of deleting either one.

The usable-set election floor: after the normalized collision makes both application/json spellings unusable, application/vnd.safe+json is the map's exactly-one USABLE concrete alternative and self-selects with no requestMedia configuration, per the amended sole-concrete gloss (exactly one usable entry self-selects; supplied values never elect). [Pins the ratified usable-set election ruling.]

A consumer-supplied Server Variable value outside the declaration's nonempty enum refuses before dispatch; a complete configured URL is the distinct replacement lane, not permission to weaken the selected Server Object.

A declaration-derived query-bearing Server alternative is excluded at that smallest owner; with no sibling or configured recovery, the represented target refuses while awaiting configuration.server The same represented target can proceed with a conforming complete URL, so this missing context is the context-required refusal species.

A declaration-derived fragment-bearing Server alternative is excluded at that smallest owner; with no sibling or configured recovery, the represented target refuses while awaiting configuration.server The same represented target can proceed with a conforming complete URL, so this missing context is the context-required refusal species.

A complete configured HTTPS URL recovers a target whose sole declaration-derived Server alternative is unusable, while leaving method, path, parameters, body, response, and security semantics unchanged.
Two complete security alternatives require an explicit configuration.security choice even when runtime credentials could satisfy both; artifact order creates no preference and nothing dispatches.
An effective empty security array is a complete no-security alternative: it self-selects, dispatches, and never volunteers unrelated runtime credential material.
A query apiKey comes only from runtime credential context, never the caller envelope, and every reserved, space, and non-ASCII UTF-8 byte is percent-encoded under Section 8.2.
An apiKey cookie value containing a semicolon is not an RFC 6265 cookie-value; it refuses before dispatch and is never percent-encoded into an invented recovery.
A credential/header-parameter collision makes only that security alternative unusable; explicitly selecting the non-colliding alternative emits only its credential and dispatches.
Raw-Cookie and structured-cookie declarations alone exclude nothing: when the invocation supplies only the structured cookie parameter, the operation completes and emits that cookie.
With the same raw-Cookie and structured-cookie declarations, supplying both values refuses before dispatch rather than parsing or merging the raw Cookie string.
A required requestBody declaration on GET is ignored by the 3.0 method-disposition rule: no body input is required and no body or Content-Type is emitted.
Supplying body on GET refuses before dispatch even when the ignored 3.0 requestBody declaration would otherwise describe it.

Accept, Content-Type, and Authorization Header Parameter declarations are ignored only as parameters: artifact-selected body media still emits Content-Type, a selected apiKey credential may emit Authorization, and this operation has no admitted response-body lane from which to generate Accept.
A supplied JSON number on a 3.0 schema-form Parameter refuses when parameterConversion is not configured; no canonical numeric spelling is inferred.
A whole JSON null on the 3.0 form-query style path uses the corrected undefined cell and emits q= rather than disappearing or entering parameterConversion.
A null member of a supplied 3.0 array Parameter has no RFC 6570 member representation and refuses before dispatch.
A selected 3.0 Parameter Object declaring both schema and content is upstream-invalid and removes the target before caller values are inspected.
A 3.0 path Parameter whose name has no corresponding path-template expression is upstream-invalid and removes the selected target as invalid.
A supplied empty string for a query Parameter with allowEmptyValue true emits a present zero-length q value; absence and empty remain distinct.
An optional 3.0 form-style cookie array remains represented, and omitting it dispatches without a Cookie field.
A typeless 3.0 exploded cookie survives static proof, but a supplied array that actually produces multiple pairs refuses at invocation time.
A 3.0 nullable string declaration still has string as its sole non-null type and therefore admits the text/plain character-data lane.
An application/xml media alternative governed by an object declaration is excluded because the OAS XML Object does not determine complete document bytes.
A supplied 3.0 nullable property on the content-based form-urlencoded path is elided as an omitted optional member and contributes no field.
An explicit 3.0 Encoding style selects the RFC 6570 path, where a supplied nullable primitive follows the form-style undefined cell and emits note= instead of being blanket-elided.
Encoding style, explode, and allowReserved are ignored for 3.0 multipart: an object property remains one JSON part under its property name rather than becoming RFC 6570 fields.
A format byte multipart part with an explicit Encoding Content-Transfer-Encoding Header schema admitting base64 emits exactly Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64.
A format byte multipart part whose explicit Encoding Content-Transfer-Encoding Header schema disallows base64 refuses when that part would be emitted.
A relative Server URL declared in an external Path Item resolves against that containing document before the operation path is joined at the server/path boundary.
configuration.implicitConnectionScope=referring resolves a 3.0 Security Requirement name in the external document containing the selected operation rather than the entry document.

A nonempty requirement array for a 3.0 non-OAuth scheme is an upstream-invalid declaration that removes that security alternative from selection before any runtime credential is inspected; every remaining complete alternative survives, so an explicitly selected empty-array alternative still dispatches.
A supplied JSON number for a 3.0 content-based form property refuses when parameterConversion is not configured; the form lane has no partial canonicalization fallback.
A 3.0 root webhooks spelling creates no binding behavior: the selected paths operation remains independently invocable and dispatches no reverse dependency.
A non-transfer Encoding Header Object is descriptive at the 3.0 operation boundary: it neither requires caller input nor makes the multipart alternative unusable.

Two Paths keys with equivalent templated hierarchies but different template names are upstream-invalid: each selected operation on a participating Path Item is removed as invalid before any caller value is inspected, even though every other declaration on that operation is intact and a non-conflicting sibling path is declared alongside it.

The equivalent-hierarchy exclusion is confined to the participating Path Items: a non-conflicting sibling path declared in the same Paths Object still resolves and dispatches, so the defect never reaches the whole source.

An admitted exact key whose value is not a Response Object retains precedence and remains an invalid response alternative, but it does not remove the target; an empty successful response dispatches and completes with no output.
A non-map response links member is confined to unused coverage; the valid sibling content declaration still governs and decodes the successful JSON response.
A response defect confined to one target does not affect a sibling operation in the same source; selecting the intact sibling still resolves, dispatches, and completes.

A defect in a Response Object that can never govern a 2xx — here an exact 404 — does not remove the target, because failure data is best-effort. The target whose success path is intact still resolves and dispatches; synthesis separately accounts the invalid 404 Response projection as coverage loss.

A request selection made through a range-keyed declaration emits the concrete requestMedia choice that instantiated it as the request Content-Type, never the range key, which names no concrete representation (§9.1's Content-Type emission pin).

The emitted request Content-Type is the elected media type in its parsed form: type and subtype are emitted in lowercase whatever spelling the declaration key used. Which spelling matched never changes the emitted bytes (§9.1's emitted-spelling pin, RFC 9110 §8.3.1).

Every media-type parameter name is emitted in lowercase and each parameter value is emitted in the characters the declaration supplied AFTER unquoting, re-quoted only where the token production does not admit it; utf-8 is a token, so the quoted declaration value emits unquoted (§9.1's emitted-spelling pin over RFC 9110 §§5.6.6, 8.3.1).

A media-type parameter other than charset compares by exact character sequence, so a case-differing requestMedia choice matches no declaration and the unmatched choice refuses before dispatch. RFC 9110 §5.6.6 leaves parameter-value case sensitivity to each parameter's own definition and RFC 2046 §4.1.2 marks charset as the only exception (§9.1's parameter-comparison pin).

A multipart entity is framed under RFC 9110 §8.3.3 and RFC 2046 §5.1.1: the emitted media type carries the generated boundary parameter, each part carries Content-Disposition: form-data with the schema-property name as a QUOTED-STRING, only CRLF represents a line break between body parts, and the entity closes with CRLF, two hyphens, the boundary value and a final two hyphens (§9.3's entity-framing rule and its quoted-name pin).

A successful response whose single Content-Type field value is a list of media types selects no media type and is a loud protocol error. RFC 9110 §8.3 defines Content-Type as one media type and defines no resolution for the list shape; the application/octet-stream assumption applies only when the field is absent.

On an UNSUCCESSFUL response the same list-valued Content-Type matches no governing content declaration, so the best-effort failure-body rule yields no failure-data value and raises no loud protocol error: the interaction simply completes unsuccessfully (§9.5's repeated/list-valued Content-Type rule, second limb).

A JSON-lane number carrying more precision than binary64 holds never fails or refuses for precision alone: §9.2's permitted set has exactly two members, preserving the supplied mathematical value or reducing it to the nearest binary64 value, and refusal is in neither. The corpus carriage itself reduces the literal, so this scenario pins the no-refusal half of that set rather than discriminating its two members.

A supplied array with ZERO members is an undefined value under RFC 6570 §2.3 — 'A variable defined as a list value is considered undefined if the list contains zero members' — and therefore uses the effective style's undefined cell, which for form is ?color= read under §8.2's presentational-prefix rule (§8.2's three-member undefined-value pin, second member).

A supplied object with ZERO members is an undefined value under RFC 6570 §2.3 — 'an associative array ... is considered undefined if the array contains zero members' — and uses the same form undefined cell (§8.2's three-member undefined-value pin, third member).

The undefined cell is looked up by the effective style, not fixed to one spelling: an empty array on a matrix path parameter emits the matrix undefined cell ';name' rather than form's 'name=' (§8.2's undefined-value rules against the OAS 3.0.4 Style Examples table).

The n/a-cell refusal reaches EVERY undefined value and not JSON null alone: spaceDelimited with explode false is a supported combination whose array column carries real bytes but whose undefined column is n/a, so a supplied empty array refuses before dispatch at that parameter (§8.2's undefined-value n/a rule, generalized from null by the chain-trace repair).

A Schema Object default documents what the receiver assumes and is never inserted by this binding: an unsupplied optional parameter carrying a default is omitted before serialization exactly as one carrying none, so no query component appears at all (§8.1's default-never-inserted rule).

The same default-never-inserted rule holds inside a request body: an object property carrying a default that the caller did not supply is not synthesized into the emitted JSON value (§8.1's default-never-inserted rule at a §9.2 JSON-lane body).

A location-only entry document passes the SAME §3.1 grammar gate as string content: the multi-document YAML stream §3.1 refuses is refused at load when it arrives by dereference rather than embedded. §5.1's retrieval-decode pin states the scope as every retrieval and not the secondary ones alone.

info:
  title: T
  version: '1'
servers:
  - url: https://api.example
paths:
  /x:
    get:
      responses:
        '204':
          description: ok
---
second: document

scenarios.description: OAS states normatively that keys used in YAML maps MUST be limited to a scalar string as defined by the YAML Failsafe schema ruleset, and section 3.1 now follows it: the Failsafe ruleset's only scalar tag is tag:yaml.org,2002:str, so every scalar key satisfies the qualifier, an unquoted Responses key is the string it spells, and the document loads. This is the common OpenAPI YAML idiom; the earlier reading refused it.

source.content:
openapi: 3.0.4
info:
  title: T
  version: '1'
servers:
  - url: https://api.example
paths:
  /x:
    get:
      responses:
        204:
          description: ok

scenarios.description: The quoted-key pair of the preceding scenario: an explicitly quoted Responses key is a scalar string under any ruleset, so it loads and dispatches. Together the pair pins that quoting is optional rather than load-bearing, which is what following the edition's Failsafe key rule means.

openapi: 3.0.4
info:
  title: T
  version: '1'
servers:
  - url: https://api.example
paths:
  /x:
    get:
      responses:

scenarios.description: Elective retrieval on a content-carrying source is never observable: content remains the interpreted artifact and is never silently replaced, so a processor that dereferences the co-present location and one that declines differ in no result this specification defines. The location here answers with a DIFFERENT artifact naming another server; the completed target still comes from content (§4's composition rule).

A selector reaching no addressable target DOES NOT RESOLVE and the invocation refuses AT RESOLUTION — the outcome §3.2's vocabulary added, distinct from an addressable target that is unusable, because no target is reached at all. The path exists and the method does not.

The operation path joins the expanded Server URL by removing exactly the redundant seam slash, with no relative URL resolution or other slash normalization: a trailing Server slash and leading Paths-key slash produce one slash.

A Security Scheme Object that is not one — here an apiKey declaration missing the REQUIRED name its type demands — is upstream-invalid and removes every security alternative naming it as invalid BEFORE any runtime credential is inspected. Every remaining complete alternative survives, so the sibling alternative is left sole and selects itself (§11's Security Scheme Object required-field rule).

A target left with no complete alternative after the upstream-invalid security alternative is removed is itself excluded under §3.2's smallest-owner rule, and a selector naming that excluded target still resolves while the invocation refuses before dispatch (§11's Security Scheme Object required-field rule against §3.2's exclusion rule).

Accept is a binding-owned credential destination even when this target's generated response-media set is empty, so an apiKey credential targeting it makes the selected alternative unusable and the sole-alternative invocation refuses before dispatch.

A supplied request value at a raw-octet boundary that is not a JSON string refuses before dispatch at the affected body; the value never reaches the wire in a repaired form (§9.2's raw-octet boundary rule).

A supplied raw-octet string that §9.2's canonical RFC 4648 §4 reading does not decode — here a one-character quantum with neither the required padding nor a whole group — refuses before dispatch rather than being repaired or partially decoded (§9.2's raw-octet boundary rule).
A plain scalar key never refuses on its resolved type, whichever Core-schema tag that resolution assigns: an unquoted true in key position is the member name it spells, and the document loads.

x-vendor:

scenarios.description: What refuses at the key gate is a key that is no scalar at all. A sequence in key position is no representation of a JSON member name and refuses at load.

The invoke half of the unsatisfiable-property accounting: the part `bad` admits no instance, so it is not a routed field, and a value supplied for it fails every admission test and refuses before dispatch at that part (Section 5.2). No request is emitted. A processor that dropped the value silently and dispatched the remaining parts would be sending a request the caller did not describe; one that excluded the target at synthesis would have removed an operation on a defect nothing reaches (the companion synthesis scenario pins that half).

expected.description: No request is emitted: the supplied `bad` value reaches a part no value can satisfy.

scenarios.description: A supplied empty string for a query Parameter that declares no allowEmptyValue serializes as the form row's empty cell, q=: the edition's Style Examples define the empty string's bytes independently of allowEmptyValue, and the empty string is not undefined.

A body-free invocation of a `trace` target whose Operation declares an optional `requestBody` dispatches with method TRACE, no body, and no Content-Type field. Section 7: the binding emits no body on `trace` because a TRACE client MUST NOT send a message body (RFC 7231 Section 4.3.8), and Content-Type indicates the media type of the associated representation (RFC 7231 Section 3.1.1.5), so a request carrying no representation carries no such field. The same wire fact is pinned on every 3.x sibling; OAPI32-PS-35 pins the required-body cell on 3.2. Whether a runtime's platform HTTP API can send TRACE at all is a host limit outside this specification: a runtime that cannot refuses before dispatch, and never dispatches another method in its place.

A required request body with two usable concrete media alternatives and no requestMedia choice is context-required before dispatch. The portable scenario asserts only the binding-specification outcome; target, durability, and challenge-record layout belong to an invocation interface's own conformance suite.

A 3.0 content-based form property whose propertyMedia choice selects application/json carries the supplied array as its JSON image, and a configured parameterConversion is never consulted: Section 8.1 names the converter only where a form/part property must convert a JSON scalar to a string, and Section 9.3 routes the property's serialization through Section 9.2's lane for the selected media type, whose JSON pin serializes the supplied value as strict JSON.

A 3.0 content-based form property whose explicit single concrete Encoding contentType is application/json carries a supplied integer and boolean as their JSON images with a configured parameterConversion never consulted; only a property routed through the text/plain lane must convert a JSON scalar to a string under Section 8.1, and Section 9.3 routes the property's serialization through Section 9.2's lane for the selected media type.

A body-free invocation of a `trace` target whose Operation declares a `required: true` requestBody dispatches with method TRACE, no body, and no Content-Type field, the required-declaration companion of OAPI30-PS-165. Section 7: on such a content-forbidding method the artifact's `required: true` request body creates no caller-body requirement, so a body-free invocation dispatches and the preceding `incorporated` rule's missing-required-body refusal does not reach it; the target is therefore invocable, not permanently unusable. The ground is RFC 7231 Section 4.3.8: a client MUST NOT send a message body in a TRACE request, so no declaration can oblige the caller to supply one. OAPI32-PS-35 pins the same cell on 3.2. The declaration is reported as coverage loss at the Request Body position, a synthesis observation outside this processor scenario's assertions. Whether a runtime's platform HTTP API can send TRACE at all is a host limit outside this specification: a runtime that cannot refuses before dispatch, and never dispatches another method in its place.

info.title: TRACE with a required body declaration

scenarios.description: Strict-JSON response parsing resolves duplicate object member names by taking the lexically last member, inside RFC 8259 Section 4's permitted receiver set. The 3.0-line twin of OAPI31-PS-118: §9.2's strict-JSON pin is identical on both lines, so the same wire fact is asserted here rather than left to the sibling.

A leading byte-order mark on a JSON response body is ignored under RFC 8259 Section 8.1's parser latitude and is never part of the value: the body parses to exactly the value that follows the mark. The 3.0-line twin of OAPI31-PS-121.

A lone surrogate escape in a JSON response body yields no value: it is a loud protocol error after a 2xx final status, because neither silent replacement of the escape nor invalid-Unicode passthrough preserves the supplied text. The 3.0-line twin of OAPI31-PS-122.

Appended is pinned here to one and only one seam repair: the implied root server and the Paths key are joined by removing only their redundant seam slash. A Paths key beginning // therefore retains its intentional doubled slash, distinguishing the narrow join from both verbatim concatenation and broad slash normalization.
The accepted OAS 3.0 editions do not forbid a path-template expression from occurring more than once. Its one effective path Parameter supplies the same value at every occurrence.
A path-template expression with no corresponding effective path Parameter is upstream-invalid and removes the selected target as invalid.
A required Request Body Object with an empty content map leaves no candidate media type, so the addressable target is excluded and invocation refuses before caller values or dispatch.
A required nullable content-based form property cannot be represented by elision; supplying null refuses before dispatch instead of silently producing the same wire form as omission.
An API-key security alternative whose declared header destination is not an HTTP token is excluded before any credential value is inspected.
A 204 response cannot carry content. Even when the governing Response Object declares text content, actual response bytes are a loud protocol error and are never decoded into an output value.
A non-token optional ordinary Header Parameter is excluded only at that projection; omitting it leaves the operation dispatchable.
The would-be caller key of an excluded optional non-token Header Parameter is unknown input and refuses before dispatch.
A non-token required ordinary Header Parameter excludes its addressable target, whose invocation refuses before dispatch.
An ordinary Header Parameter cannot give the caller control of Transfer-Encoding; the addressable target is excluded and refuses before dispatch.
A 101 response is an immediate loud response-phase protocol error because this unary binding has no upgraded-protocol continuation; the processor does not wait for another HTTP response.

A non-HTTP artifact Server does not destroy the addressable or represented operation, but the artifact-derived completed target refuses before dispatch. The same represented target can proceed with a conforming complete URL, so this missing context is the context-required refusal species.
A complete configured HTTPS URL replaces a non-HTTP artifact Server and dispatches the otherwise unchanged operation.
A non-token optional cookie Parameter is excluded only at that projection; omitting it leaves the operation dispatchable.
The would-be caller key of an excluded optional non-token cookie Parameter is unknown input and refuses before dispatch.
A non-token required cookie Parameter excludes its addressable target, whose invocation refuses before dispatch.
A non-token required response Header Object key excludes its response alternative; a successful response governed by it is a loud response-phase protocol error.
A content-form cookie Parameter whose exact serialized value is not an RFC 6265 cookie-value refuses before dispatch; the binding neither escapes nor repairs it.
A default-only Responses Object is valid, and its fallback Response Object governs an otherwise unmatched successful status.
A leading SP is field-line whitespace rather than part of an RFC 9110 field-value, so an ordinary Header Parameter cannot preserve it and refuses before dispatch.
A raw Cookie Header Parameter must serialize to a complete RFC 6265 cookie-string; a value without a cookie-pair refuses before dispatch.
A header apiKey credential ending in HTAB is not an RFC 9110 field-value and refuses before dispatch.
A selected header apiKey named Cookie is a raw Cookie source; combining it with a supplied structured cookie Parameter refuses before dispatch.
A selected header apiKey named Cookie and a selected cookie apiKey in the same AND requirement are raw and structured Cookie sources; combining them refuses before dispatch.
ASCII-case variants denote one response field: one received field discharges the group and the complete Content-Encoding value satisfies every binding-understood finite constraint.
Case-equivalent required Encoding headers with conflicting exact artifact values exclude the multipart alternative rather than selecting a key by case or map order.
An omitted optional parameter creates no collision; the selected credential emits once and dispatches.
A supplied optional parameter and selected credential that reach the same actual field refuse before dispatch.
An exploded runtime object is not statically excluded, but its actual serialized token destination collides with the selected query credential and refuses before dispatch.
A required ordinary Proxy-Authorization parameter is excluded at the target boundary because that field authenticates to the first inbound proxy, not the origin API.
Ordinary and credential query contributions form one unordered multiset while preserving each contribution's encoded bytes.
An anonymous TRACE alternative survives and dispatches without volunteered credential fields.
A TRACE target whose sole alternative emits a credential refuses before dispatch.
A generated multipart name uses UTF-8, emits qdtext literally, and escapes only DQUOTE and backslash with one quoted-pair.
A followed cross-origin redirect strips binding-selected header credentials and does not append the original query credential to the Location target.
Supplying request Content-Encoding on an invocation that emits no request representation refuses before dispatch.
A case-insensitive HTTP bearer scheme consumes one valid b64token and constructs the exact Authorization field.
A valid OAuth2 Bearer token uses the same exact RFC 6750 Authorization construction.
A valid OpenID Connect Bearer token uses the same exact RFC 6750 Authorization construction.
An empty HTTP bearer credential cannot satisfy b64token and refuses before dispatch.
A space inside an OAuth2 access token is outside b64token and refuses before dispatch.
CR/LF in an OpenID Connect token is outside b64token and refuses before dispatch without emitting a field.
An explicitly non-Bearer OAuth2 runtime token has no carriage under this identifier and refuses before dispatch.

HEAD carries a syntactically valid, declaration-admitted Content-Encoding field but no content octets. The installed Brotli decoder fails if called, so successful empty completion proves the method-based no-content rule does not invoke it.

A 304 response carries a syntactically valid, declaration-admitted Content-Encoding field but no content octets. A failing Brotli sentinel is installed, but the no-content rule does not invoke it. Because 304 is not successful, completion remains the native unsuccessful response.

A non-UTF-8 character request lane requires its direction-specific encoder. With no such runtime capability, encoding refuses before dispatch rather than being reported as a response error or silently substituted.

On a successful HEAD response, resolving the Header schema $ref and filtering the mixed enum yields the exact domain containing only identity. The wire value 7 therefore fails; ignoring the reference or stringifying the numeric enum member would incorrectly complete.

A Server Variable Object missing its REQUIRED default is upstream-invalid at the Server alternative. With no surviving declaration-derived alternative or configured recovery, invocation refuses before dispatch. The same represented target can proceed with a conforming complete URL, so this missing context is the context-required refusal species.

A successful HEAD response still validates Content-Encoding field grammar before the no-content rule suppresses decoding; a non-token coding-list member fails loudly even though no decoder is invoked.
A successful HEAD response still applies its governing exact raw-string Content-Encoding domain; gzip is outside the declared br domain and fails loudly without invoking a content decoder.

Request and response character codecs are independent directional capabilities. The request encoder is installed and permits dispatch, while the response decoder is a failing sentinel and therefore produces a loud response-phase error.

A successful HEAD response evaluates nested allOf constraints recursively. The outer domain admits identity or br, but the nested exact domain admits only identity, so br fails; a shallow implementation would incorrectly complete.
An empty Server Variable enum excludes only that Server alternative; the represented target remains context-required on configuration.server.

scenarios.description: A declaration default outside its nonempty Server Variable enum excludes only that Server alternative; the represented target remains context-required on configuration.server.

scenarios.description: A URL expression without a matching Server Variable declaration is not excluded, but an invocation that supplies no exact substitution is context-required on configuration.server.

scenarios.description: A Server Variable Object with a wrong-typed REQUIRED default is upstream-invalid at its Server alternative; the represented target remains context-required on configuration.server.

scenarios.description: A 204 response carries a syntactically valid, declaration-admitted Content-Encoding field but no content octets. The installed Brotli decoder fails if called, so successful empty completion proves the status-based no-content rule does not invoke it.

Case-equivalent response Header declarations govern conjunctively rather than by first-key selection. The first identity domain admits the actual field, but the second br domain rejects it, so the response fails loudly.

Case-equivalent response Header declarations govern conjunctively rather than by last-key selection. The first br domain rejects the actual field, although the second identity domain admits it, so the response fails loudly.

A caller-supplied JSON request value containing one unpaired surrogate code unit refuses before dispatch. The corpus materializes U+D800 after parsing its JSON-safe template so neither U+FFFD replacement nor an emitted lone-surrogate escape can masquerade as the supplied value.

An excluded optional non-token header projection sharing its declared name with a surviving query parameter is removed before caller-key uniqueness is computed; the surviving query parameter therefore uses its unqualified key and dispatches.
Because the removed header projection does not activate qualified mode, the would-be qualified query key is unknown input and refuses before dispatch.

Every admitted response-content media alternative is advertised once at equal preference in deterministic normalized order, while a case-insensitive q parameter is confined to its excluded alternative and cannot become an Accept weight.
A generated multipart Content-Disposition carries the declared part name and invents neither filename nor filename*.
An admissible artifact-fixed Content-Disposition may carry a literal filename and is emitted verbatim rather than replaced or derived from the supplied value.
An artifact-fixed multipart Content-Disposition containing filename* excludes that media alternative under RFC 7578 and refuses before dispatch when it is the only required request lane.
A present caller-envelope value that is not a JSON object is outside the closed envelope grammar and refuses before dispatch; it is never treated as a body value or parameter map.
An optional exploded form-cookie array remains represented, and a supplied one-item value emits exactly one Cookie pair.
A required non-exploded form-cookie array remains represented, and a supplied one-item value emits one valid Cookie pair.
A typeless non-exploded form-cookie declaration survives static analysis, but a supplied array reaches OAS 3.0's unsupported multi-value Cookie representation and refuses.
A nested runtime object under a typeless deepObject member leaves the admitted scalar-member cell and refuses without private stringification.
A required Request Body whose sole object-model XML alternative is excluded has no surviving effective request-content alternative and excludes the target.
Accept advertises admitted media from both success and failure Responses, but a failure-only problem media type cannot govern an actual 200 response.
A required exploded form-cookie object remains represented, and a supplied one-property value emits exactly one Cookie pair under that property's name.
A supplied empty array is present rather than omitted and uses the form undefined-value cell, emitting one empty Cookie pair rather than disappearing or entering the multi-value refusal path.
